Mortify

MOR-tuh-fy · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To mortify is to embarrass, shame, or humiliate someone severely.

Being mortified in front of the whole cafeteria was worse than any punishment the principal could have given her.

Worked Example

The senator was utterly mortified when a hot mic caught him singing off-key backstage, and the clip aired on every news channel that night.

Mortify describes a severe, often public humiliation -- much stronger than simple embarrassment.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

humiliate: to cause someone to feel ashamed or foolish

abash: to embarrass or disconcert someone

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

reassure: to say or do something to remove someone's doubts or fears

gratify: to give pleasure or satisfaction to someone

Where it sits · how crushing the shame is — embarrass → mortify → humiliate

embarrass vs. mortify: To embarrass is weaker than to mortify: forgetting a name is a small, quickly forgotten embarrassment, while being mortified means shame so intense you wish the floor would swallow you.

humiliate vs. mortify: To humiliate someone often means a deeper, more deliberate loss of dignity than a moment of mortification.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — mort-

root — mort-: death (Latin mors, mortis)

suffix — -ify

suffix — -ify: to make or cause to become (Latin -ficare)

Put it together

Put it together: Mortify comes from Latin mort- ("death") + -ify ("to make") -- literally "to make dead," which came to mean a shame so severe it feels like dying of embarrassment.

Use the root in a new word: mortal

Use the root in a new word: mortal: Even superheroes are mortal in the end, unable to escape death forever.

Word Choice

Mortify is a strong word -- reserve it for humiliation intense enough that the person wished they could disappear, not everyday embarrassment.
